1. The animation shows a grid of squares, where each square stands for one historical US scenario. Light squares are scenarios where the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark squares are scenarios where the renter was ahead. The labels cite FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The grid is marked "illustrative" and "US only · history, not a forecast." A caption gives "buyer ahead: 73.6% · 87.3%". Two figures, 4.83% and 5.59% a year, are attributed to the Census vacancy survey. One caption says the number is "a reference, not Nina's own rent."

2. A dark column of renter-ahead squares sits in the middle of the grid and changes shape from frame to frame. It is wide in frames 1 and 2 and narrower in frames 3 to 6, and in frame 5 it is the narrowest. The light squares fill more of the grid as this happens. A small blue marker on a slider at the bottom also shifts position. It is further left in frame 1 and moves right in frames 2, 3, 5 and 6. I can't tell from the image alone what the slider controls. It may be the assumed rent or the assumed rate. The "buyer ahead" caption appears from frame 3, and the "reference" caption appears from frame 4.

3. Across the historical periods it draws on, buying came out ahead of renting after ten years in most cases, roughly 74% to 87% depending on the assumptions. Renting came out ahead in a minority, shown by the dark squares. How big that minority is depends on the inputs, such as rent level and rate. The two percentages most likely correspond to two settings, but the image doesn't say which. The figures describe the past and are not a forecast.

4. The image gives no direct advice. A viewer would probably take away that buying has more often beaten renting over a ten-year horizon. They would also take away that the result depends on rent and rates, and that their own rent may differ from the reference figure.

5. The advice in 4 is my own reading. The on-screen text only reports the percentages and cautions that this is history, not a forecast, and that the rent is only a reference. It doesn't tell the viewer to buy or rent.
